lessons.t: $100M Sales Teams 1 — Start Here: Strategy, Frame & Script (~75 min)
lessons.md:
- **Credentials**: 15 years in sales and 4,000+ deals Alex closed himself. He went from barely closing free trials, to a mobile team launching gyms in six new markets a month, to a 30-person inbound/outbound B2B team, to a phone team that closed 1,000+ sales in 72 hours during the Guinness-record book launch. He has personally done every role: seller, trainer, manager and recruiter of recruiters. **"The hardest thing in entrepreneurship is learning what good looks like."** This course gives you the pattern for each role.
- **Culture frame (from ACQ's internal handbook, paraphrased)**:
- The fraternity-pledge story: the new class wanted to quit. Alex asked who still wanted what they'd joined for, then told them "this is what hard feels like." The choice is whether you quit when it's hard or get harder.
- To be top 1% / 0.1% / 0.01%, you have to walk into a room of 100 / 1,000 / 10,000 people and come out #1. You can't be exceptional and live a normal life, so stop explaining yourself to people who don't support you.
- The "secret": **get better and never stop.** The work begins when motivation ends.
- The best way to become a champion is to join a championship team. If your team won't hit the standard, you're the problem, and you have to live it first.
- The system hasn't changed in years. Human persuasion and human learning don't change; only the tech does. **"Being advanced is just never skipping the basics."** Founder-led sales convert well because founders do the basics, so get everyone else doing them too.
- Course structure: strategy → **recruiting → training → managing**.

## Prerequisites before you recruit: a FRAME and a SCRIPT

- Alex's early ego said no one could sell like him. Over Christmas 2013, his tanning-salon partner wrote a script, taught it to staff, and they went **2 for 5** the first day. That was the first money that ever came into the business without Alex.
- Objections and answers:
- "Don't sound scripted" → they only sound scripted if they read it. Once they know it, add active listening (repeat their last words back with an upward tone).
- "Every situation is unique" → **every closed sale is the same; every botched sale is different.** Either you write the script or the rep makes one up. Which do you trust more?
- "No one can sell like me" → they can't sell like you, but they can sell as well as you if you use a **process frame instead of an authority frame**. ACQ's reps are mostly 19–22 and sell to owners of $1M–$100M businesses.
- **Secretary/nurse protecting the surgeon** frame: the rep only checks fit.
- **Mechanic** frame: "we have to pop the hood before we can tell you what's needed."
- "Long, multi-call cycle" → about 80% of enterprise sales are the same pitch repeated up the chain to the decision maker. Truly different steps just need different scripts.
- A script + frame means fewer qualifications are needed, faster onboarding, more predictability and lower cost. **Golf analogy**: don't teach every club; put the ball 6 inches from the hole and have reps practise that putt all day. Don't make reps be therapist, teacher and consultant. Reps sell; the education happens before the call.

## The FRAME: VSLs (video sales letters) — the "VSL sandwich"

- Give as much information as possible before the conversation. Under-educated prospects are why you need multiple calls. This can **double or triple** sales efficiency (fewer, better-paid reps).
- **VSL structure** (just record it on a phone; it's mostly a **"proof salad"**, proof presented many different ways so viewers see themselves in it: same demographics, beliefs, behaviours, outcomes):
- **Intro (~60s)**: promise → pain → proof ("you don't have to believe me", plus varied case studies) → plan → picture (visual roadmap).
- **Core persuasion**: **old way vs new way** (them vs us = your unique mechanism).
- **Objections/FAQs 1…n**: what they believe → why it's wrong → what's right → proof. Treat it as a living document and splice in new objections the reps hear.
- **CTA** that personalizes the next call (e.g. "how many square feet is your kitchen?" "how many cars fit in the driveway?"), which also proves they watched.
- **Proof gauntlet**: a long run of happy-customer stories. In person, hand them an iPad and say "the back 15 minutes are just customer stories"; people keep watching anyway.
- **Placement**: at every step, especially **zero-friction points** (after an opt-in or booking, where they can't drop out). Keep it **short before a friction point** (each minute costs leads) and as long as you like after it.
- Flow: ad → page (with VSL) → BANT questions → scheduler with proof → post-booking VSL (to drive show-up) → speed-to-lead call to confirm.
- On the call: "Did you watch the video? It's 10 minutes and saves us 35 on the call."
- Home services: **never email a quote later.** Play a VSL on an iPad while you walk to the truck, then come back and close.
- Two levers in any sales motion: **education** (right information) and **qualification** (right person; add **BANT friction: budget, authority, need, timing**). Closing 0 of 100 usually means you're talking to the wrong people.
- Alex runs ~50 active VSLs and films 2–3 new or updated ones each week, with paths per avatar.

## The SCRIPT: Intro → Disco → Pitch → Close (or the CLOSER framework; pick one)

- **90% of scripts improve when you cut 50–75%.** Fast reinforcement teaches false lessons (the "sneeze before the offer" superstition). Aim for **word concision**: a 20–30-minute call instead of 45 doubles team efficiency (20 reps instead of 40). Goal: the highest revenue per rep in the industry.
- **Intro** (US compliance "big four": name, company, recorded line, reason for the call) → small yes → set the agenda ("I'll ask some questions to make sure it's a fit; if so I'll walk you through it and, if it makes sense, get you set up — sound good?"). Skip the weather talk.
- **Disco** (the most important part; nail it and the pitch and close become easy):
- **Current vs desired state** (the gap). Don't move on until there's a gap.
- **Pain cycle ("pulling teeth")**: obstacle → "why?" → get specific with **"Tell me more about that." / "Can you give me an example?"** (commands, which keep a subtle authoritative frame). Lack of urgency means you didn't dig enough into the pain. Deprivation creates motivation.
- **Recap → label → confirm**: "So it sounds like the real issue isn't the vendors, it's that you need a whole new marketing and sales process. Does that sound right?"
- Example: the weight-loss prospect who eats fast food during the kids' soccer practices.
- **Pitch** (≤2 minutes; they care about themselves, not you): "Given everything you told me, I think [X] would help. Mind if I walk you through it?" Then **problem → solution → benefit ×3**, confirming each ("do you think that would help?"). **Edify the expert** who will deliver (director of marketing, director of weight loss). The closer doesn't need to be the expert.
- **Close**: if they already know the price range, "ready to get started?" Otherwise use **"Sounds good so far? … It is expensive — it's $8,000."** (heard from a Vegas helicopter-tour seller: broke buyers brace for it, rich buyers find it less than they expected.) Then **shut up**. Reps who wait **8+ seconds close ~30% more**; Alex has sat through 2+ minutes of silence.
- **Tonality**: always be loud, slow and clear enough. **Pause to emphasize; raise your pitch to solicit a response.** The ask gets both. Scripts mark short, medium and long pauses (long = wait until they speak).
- **Analogies** compress a whole lifetime of experience into one sentence, so they're the most efficient way to transfer information:
- Multiple ways up the mountain (many ways to solve a constraint); the Don Shula frame (every play designed to score, so run them all).
- You need all of it: car wheels/engine/gas, three-legged stool.
- Constraint: weakest link, 4-lane highway into 1 lane.
- It takes time: braces, tanning in layers, building muscle.
- Price: cheapest surgeon, tattoo artist or parachute?
- Hesitation: "the water won't get warmer"; "your ship won't sink slower while you pick buckets."
- Will it work for me: "gravity doesn't care who jumps"; "follow the recipe, get the same cake."

## Closing loops (the job is handling "no"; if everyone said yes you'd be an order-taker)

- **Data: the reps who ask the most times close the most.** The skill is what to say between asks so asking again doesn't annoy people.
- **Sequence**: triage → loop 1 → 5 universal closes → **AAA** between each → 5 specific objections.
- **Loop 1 (confirm value)**: "Completely hear you. Quick question: do you think this could help you get **closer** to your goal?" (directional, so it's easy to say yes). Then ask again; this alone closes ~25%. If not: "What's your main concern? **What are you afraid of having happen?**"
- **5 universal closes** (skeleton keys; most objections aren't real, people just need to be asked again and reassured):
  1. **Reason close**: their reason not to is the reason to ("not a good time? that's exactly why you should"; "can't afford it? you need it more than anyone, and you'll care the most, so you'll get the best results").
  2. **Hypothetical close**: "If [this issue] were solved, would you do it?" Isolate it and solve it.
  3. **Zoom out / pull the parachute**: "You want weight loss, we sell weight loss. What am I missing?" This gets you out of the dogfight (even if you win the argument, you lose the sale). Follow with "Do you think hesitating in the past is part of why you're here?"
  4. **1–10 scale**: (a) "What would make it a 10?" → solve that, or flip it: "why not a 1?" so they sell themselves. (b) Whatever number they give: "you're above most people; nobody's a 10 until they've done it, so let's get you moving."
  5. **Best case / worst case**: best case your life changes; worst case you get a bunch of value (plus the guarantee). Doing nothing guarantees you don't get what you came for. Sales is reducing risk, so **show that inaction is the riskier option.**
- **AAA between loops: Acknowledge, Associate, Ask.** "Totally get that, and believe it or not that's exactly what our best clients asked…" then the next close. Associate the objection with buyers, compliment them, and stay in the pocket.
- **Make no statements, only questions** ("be like water/smoke"). Prospects disbelieve what you say and believe what they say. Never prove them wrong. Give them trapdoors that save face. Use a **foil**: "Mind if I share what I told a guy just like you last week who then crushed it?" That lets you say harsher truths.
- **5 specific objections** (most are smoke screens for money):
- **Time** = priorities, not time. **When-then fallacy** ("I'll go to the hospital once I'm healthy"). Starting while busy is better because you're most motivated and it becomes permanent. Ask what younger you would say. "What's the least important thing you do? Trade that."
- **Money** = value. **The Ferrari test**: a legit Ferrari offered for $5k, and they'd find the money. Frames:
- It's good that it's a lot.
- Knock off a zero: would you even believe it?
- "If all it did was X, would it be worth it?"
- The fur-coat salesman: "If it were free, would you take one? Then it's not about the money…"
- "Can you do it for less?" → laugh, "I could do it for more!"
- "Others are cheaper": if same price, which would you pick? Good/fast/cheap, pick two.
- Money is spent either way; it's just which goal it moves you toward.
- If they truly lack money: **resourcefulness, not resources**. Brainstorm vendors, prepays, a cash campaign to cover the first payment.
- **Decision maker** (confirm all decision makers attend ahead of time):
  1. "What if they say no?" ("I'd do it anyway" closes ~1 in 3.)
  2. "What specifically would they object to?" (puts it back on the person present).
  3. "Do they approve of your current situation? Why would they oppose something that'll make you happy?"
  4. **Ask for support, not permission.**
- **Fit/preference**: you have to change to change; trade-offs ("you can't eat the cake and have the six-pack"). Is the trade worth the outcome?
- **Stall** (you're finally talking to the decision maker): quantify the cost of inaction.
- "Did hesitating before lead you here?"
- "**Burned twice**": did you marry the first person you dated? Don't let one bad past purchase burn you twice.
- **3 decisions**: do you like the product, the company, me?
- **Direction, not perfection**: closer or further from your goal?
- Perfect information only exists after you've tried it (test-drive / guarantee).
- **Information, not time**: "What information do you still need?"
- "Decide" comes from the Latin for "to cut off": which future are you cutting off?
- If it's sooner or later anyway, do it sooner.
- Extrapolate the pain: "5 more years on this path, you're 250 lb. How would that feel?"
- **80/20 of closing**: ~30–40% close on the first ask; the universal loops get ~80% in total (enough to hit KPIs). The remaining ~20% of edge cases is what makes someone top 1%, at diminishing returns.
- **End of call: they buy, or time runs out.**
- If no sale, **"BAMFAM" (book a meeting from a meeting)**. Save 2–3 minutes and never hang up without the next step: "It'll save us both time, saves adding a to-do, and we can always move it." Then suggest times, ignoring the first no. Then shrink it to 15 minutes. Then "when were you planning to let me know?" and make that the meeting time. If you can't close the appointment, you won't close the sale.
- If they buy, **ask for a referral**: "Who else do you know who's as awesome as you?", then a live 3-way intro ("people who do it together get the best results"). **Referrals = 20–30% of sales**, and they close higher with no price resistance. Half are asked on the call; buyers who weren't asked go to the top of the follow-up list.
- Lock the script. Training days later map onto script sections, so every part gets trained every day.

## ---

**Who to look for**

- **Prove the process yourself before hiring.** Too many unknowns otherwise: is it the person or the process? Then **hire several people at once if cash allows.** Training five takes the same time as training one. If 2 of 5 succeed, the process works. If all 5 fail, the problem is you.
- **The 3 P's + 1**: they have sold this **prospect**, this **process** and this **product**. They need at least 2 of the 3, and prospect matters most. Also:
- Similar volume (several deals a day vs one every two weeks).
- Similar traffic temperature (referrals/organic → ads → cold calling/door-knocking).
- **At least 1 year of experience.**
- Example: Jared, a strong enterprise-SaaS rep, flopped at ACQ because he lacked the P's.
- **Intangibles**:
- **Intelligence = rate of learning.** Test by coaching them live and seeing how fast they apply feedback.
- **Work ethic.** Interview prep, script practice, quality of questions, and **how fast they follow up between steps.** During recruiting, you are their lead.
- **Humility.** Ego blocks learning (e.g. "you should change the script" from someone who's never sold your product).
- **Evolution of "attitude vs aptitude"**:
- 101: hire for the smallest skill gap.
- 301: **hire whoever needs the fewest resources to reach your standard.** Cost to get them there ≈ gap ÷ (intelligence × training quality). Smart people keep improving after they pass the standard.
- **Hiring order**:
- Low inbound flow → hire **setters** first (create demand).
- Strong inbound/organic → hire **closers** first.
- **ACQ's farm system: everyone starts as a setter (SDR); 100% of closers (BCs, "business consultants") are promoted from within.** "If you can't set, you can't close." This means faster ramp, longer tenure and fewer botched leads. ACQ hasn't fired a closer in 12+ months. Churn happens at SDR level, usually in the first 60 days.
- When remote, spread reps across time zones for coverage.
- Hiring the leader first (who builds the team) is fastest, but very hard to judge. Good salespeople can BS you.
- **Managers**: **don't promote your best closer.** Alex once did; sales fell and the team didn't improve. "The best coach (Phil Jackson) wasn't the best player."
- Look for an even-keeled person in the top ~25% who cares about growing people.
- Signs: the one others go to with questions, who stays late to help.
- Must be willing to take calls themselves and must not change everything on arrival.
- **Interview questions**:
- "What numbers do you track?" (quality and quantity of metrics) → **"How does what you do change those numbers?"** You want behaviours: modelling, role-play, incentives.
- What have you observed and corrected on a team?
- Biggest accomplishment (look for obsession).
- Biggest problem solved, specifically (real solvers give detail).
- Biggest loss and why (ownership vs victimhood).
- Favourite part of the job (team, growth).
- Traits: ownership, high standards, low ego, drive, invests in others.

## Pay

- **It's cheaper to pay better.** ACQ hires ex-top closers into setter seats and pays setters what closers earn elsewhere, so ACQ closers earn even more.
- CAC drops, ramp time drops, conversion rises and team churn drops.
- You get more and better applicants, plus **"pressure from behind"** so the team never has leverage on you.
- Fewer wasted leads, which is the biggest cost.
- **Setters and closers are both paid on closes** (ACQ tried sets and shows). This aligns incentives: setters qualify harder and handle objections, which prepares them to become closers. Exception: long enterprise cycles may pay on qualified shows.
- **OTE (on-target earnings) split 50% base / 50% variable** for inbound closers (from a Vista Equity study). The base removes "commission breath" desperation; the variable funds lifestyle.
- Don't start from "what %?" Start from the skill needed and the market pay for it.
- Example: $100k OTE → $50k base / $50k variable ≈ $1,000/week. If a rep takes 9 calls/day, 6 show and they close 2, × 6 days = 12 closes/week → **~$83 per sale**.
- **Accelerators** (once you have good metrics) keep reps from getting comfortable. Tier rates upward through the month (e.g. first 30 sales $75 → next 10 $95 → $105 → $125 → $150) so the average still comes to ~$83 but the end of the month pays most. This gamifies it.
- If you must pay a percentage, use **cash collected upfront** (or upfront gross margin), never contract value. Flat per-sale is preferred.
- Self-generating, field and outbound hunters are different: back into allowable CAC, usually uncapped.

## The 7-step recruiting machine

1. **Traffic**
2. **Application page**
3. Treat it as a sales letter, not HR copy, with a VSL on the company vision. Sections: who it's for, what we offer, what we expect, results, requirements, comp, benefits, values.
4. Brutally honest (long hours).
5. **Required 60-second selfie video**: ACQ never hired anyone who skipped it.
6. **Group first call**
7. Group calls, not 1:1. ACQ's outbound team missed hiring goals for 3 quarters because the bottleneck was 1:1 screening (20 calls → 4 passed → 1 offer). Switching to group calls hit the goal within 6 weeks, run by sales, not HR.
8. **Set expectations hard: 6 days a week, 12 hours a day.** The green flag is that 1–2 people leave the call.
9. Everyone hired was #1 on their last team. Expect 12–18 months to reach the top.
10. **"What it looks like vs feels like"**: learning is fastest early, but income comes at world-class edges, which takes boring volume ("violence of volume").
11. Show the calendar of the fastest-promoted closer: ~18 months, essentially no days off.
12. Q&A: **interrupt people to test agility.** A 60-second background plus "why ACQ" round, where you push for relevance. Results go out by text afterwards.
13. **Skills/technical call**: treat it as the first training session. Send the script beforehand; role-play and interrupt 30–40 times. **End immediately if they're unprepared or late.** Watch rate of learning, ego and follow-up. Green flags: closing questions like "What would it take to make the team? What's missing?"
14. **Culture call**: quality control against desperate managers. The interviewer **unsells until the candidate sells themselves**.
15. Looking for "psychos/maniacs" with big 5–10-year goals, 2-year short-term goals, humility.
16. "What will you do well? Where will you struggle?" → give candid feedback (e.g. "your tone sounds harsh"). If they get weird, it's a no.
17. Restate the hours: "Why would you want this?" Resell the vision to good fits. Judge the quality of their questions.
18. **Offer**: start date, relocation, **handbook + pre-work + a VSL** so they train before day 1. Check whether they did the homework.
19. (Then onboarding/training.)

## Feeding the machine

- Story: an insurance founder (~$10M) learned a mentor paid only $500 per referral for a broker worth ~$250k GP/year. He raised the internal referral bonus to **$25k** and grew to ~$400M.
- **Talent version of LTV:CAC**: (1-year GP per activated rep × % who activate) ÷ cost to acquire talent ≥ **3:1**. Example: $250k × 50% = $125k→willingtopayupto~$40k per hire. If hiring is your constraint, it's the best place to spend. **Always be hiring** (pressure from behind).
- **Sources, best first**:
- **Employee referrals**, with the bonus paid at the **activation point (~day 90)**, not hire. This creates an internal champion. Half of ACQ's media team came from referrals.
- Posting content; emailing your customer list.
- **Recruiters/headhunters**: contingency only (paid on hire, no retainers). Negotiate the rate down and **no exclusivity** ("can you get me 100 in 2 weeks? no? then not exclusive"). Use 4–10 of them and still run **your** process (group call first). ~$5–10k per sales hire is typical. One portfolio company went **0 → 50 activated reps in 90 days** (hired 80, kept 50), doing ~$5M/month on the phone.
- Paid ads/job boards: you get trash unless you're good at funnels.
- Forums/communities, sales-coaching groups, and direct outreach ("you're perfect for this role. Know a clone of you?").
- Recurring roles (editors, advisors, sales) each need their own machine. Use recruiters for one-off, non-core roles.

lessons.t: $100M Sales Teams 3 — Training: Stranger to SDR Bootcamp (~26 min)
lessons.md:
**Lifecycle (7 skills/decisions):** bootcamp (stranger → SDR in ~14 days) → ramp gates → when to cut → career path (titles + perks) → promotion SDR→closer → closer ramp.

## The bootcamp

- **Why:** new reps mixed into the team got overwhelmed by everyone's tips and tricks, which slowed training down. A friend in solar ran off-site bootcamps, so ACQ adopted **14 days of isolated, full-day training**.
- On day 1, sell them the "violence" of effort it takes by showing the fastest-promoted rep's calendar for about 2 minutes.
- **Four activities only:** game tape, script memorization, role-play, the handbook.
- **Prospect training beats product training.** Once you can sell a prospect, you can sell them anything. Selling weight loss to a 35-year-old mum of two uses the same Intro/Disco/Pitch/Close whether the offer is supplements, personal training, HRT or an app. The pitch is about 2 minutes, so most training covers their pains and **their language** (gym owners say "EFTs", not "recurring revenue"). If you sound like a foreigner, they won't believe you can help them.
- The manager role-plays with each rep **3× per day**: morning (agenda + personal coaching), midday, and end of day (review + what to practise).
- **Days 0–7:**
- Day 0: the team reaches out, weekend 1:1s, homework.
- Day 1: sell the process (values, path, brand, gates) before teaching it.
- Day 2: **Intro + early friction** ("I don't have time"). This is where confidence is built or lost.
- Day 3: **Discovery**, the heaviest day. **"The pain is the pitch."** Calls are won or lost here.
- Day 4: Bridge → pitch → booking/BAMFAM. Easy if days 2–3 went well; the pitch is fully memorized.
- Day 5: Full script under pressure.
- Day 6: First real dials.
- **Day 7: script graduation**, pass/fail on script adherence, tonality, recaps and handling the top 5 objections.
- **Days 8–14:** more phone time, shadowing live calls, game-tape reviews; tighten precision with pipelining and Q&A.
- **Daily minimum: read the script aloud 25× (~2 hours)** so the words are automatic and reps can actually listen. "Don't practise until you get it right; practise until you can't get it wrong." **Boredom means you're doing it right.** One SDR did 50 reps a day, each recorded on Loom, got bored by rep 7 on day 1, and learned the script faster than anyone in team history. **Ramp speed is directly correlated with success in the role.**
- Reps also consume Alex's books and the lead magnets prospects read.

## Role-play (the #1 training tool)

- **Frame** (what, how, why) → **Model** (the manager does it) → the rep copies → practise the fix until it's right (patient, as many reps as needed) → **recap**.
- **NPC prospects first** (scripted answers, no curveballs) until the whole flow is automatic, then add pressure.
- **Speed rounds / "dirty reps":** people go around the room each doing the next section (intro → disco → pitch → close) with no replies, for maximum volume.
- **Blackout method** for memorization (good for remote reps): print the script, read it, black out one word, read it again, and repeat for every word. This is why the script has to be correct first.
- **Day-8 cohort survey:** a private DM asking what to start, stop, continue, and what they'd like more of. Asked privately so the first answer doesn't anchor everyone. Day 8 is fresh enough to recall specifics and late enough to judge what mattered. If 3+ reps mention something, fix it in the playbook and tell the cohort. One-off issues get handled 1:1. Praise tells you what to protect.

## Ramp gates (don't throw new reps at your leads)

- One early rep did 50 connects a day, but nobody showed up. Closers got bogged down and good leads were burned.
- **Gate 1:** cap at **30 connects/day** (≈10 conversations of 3+ minutes ≈ 2–3 sets) and hold ~10 sets/week for a week.
- **Gate 2:** cap at **3 sets/day until show rate is above 60%** (target 70–75%).
- Then **open full dial time (6+ hours/day)**. Fully ramped means **12+ sets/week, >70% show rate, 3+ closes/week, within ~2 months**. Top SDRs earn ~$130k/year. Each gate cleared gets a public shout-out.
- **Outbound dial cadence:** cutting from 14 dials to 7 lost only ~10% of sales and **doubled team throughput**.
- Day 1: 3 dials + email + SMS (SMS sent instantly on opt-in).
- Day 2: 2 dials.
- Day 3: 1 dial + email + SMS.
- Day 4: 1 dial.
- Double-dial from local numbers. **An email reply triggers an immediate call.**

## When to cut

- **"Elite teams are built through elimination, not addition."** "You get the team you tolerate." A new leader kept underperforming friends; once he cut them and hired two strong reps, the team's culture was set. **Seal Team 6 of sales.**
- Keep it quantitative so nothing is a surprise.
- Behind on a ramp gate for one week → 2-week coaching plan with clear targets.
- **Bad culture fit, or can't take feedback → cut immediately.**
- **Feedback must describe observable behaviour** ("you talk too fast, you don't raise your pitch on questions, your volume rises when responding and sounds argumentative"), not "you sound like a jerk". Learning that language takes time.
- It's a **performance seat with a 60-day window**, stated on day 1 and reiterated around day 45. Extend only for exceptional, coachable, hardest-working people.
- **Most predictive day-1 red flag: a new rep trying to "improve" the script.** Nobody who did that has succeeded.

## Career path & retention

- For each repeated role: junior → mid → senior titles, each with a **pay bump and perks**. **Many small, frequent milestones beat a few big ones** (12 promotions > 2). Split raises into chunks so they have something to "write home about".
- **Perks = better leads** (tier 3 → tier 2 → tier 1, rotated monthly at the manager's discretion, so the best leads go to the best closers and lead value is maximized), better hours, and so on. Slack posts speed-to-lead by tier group every hour.
- Paths beyond closer:
- Sell bigger tickets or deals (individual-contributor track).
- Manage setters, then closers.
- Sales director at a portfolio company.
- Holding-company sales strategy / click-to-close process.
- Deal maker.
- **A high ceiling attracts stars**, even if only 1–3 people reach it. People trade short-term pay for upside because everyone thinks they're the star of their own movie.

## Promotion: SDR → closer ("undeniable")

- Being qualified ≠ being promoted. It means you're first in line for the next open seat.
- **Requirements, sustained for a full quarter:**
- All KPI minimums (6+ hours/day dialling, sets, show rate, close rate).
- 100% admin/CRM compliance with no nagging.
- No repeat process violations.
- Lives the values (competitive greatness, candour, unimpeachable character).
- **Unlocks:**
- **1 self-set per day**, closing your own sets.
- First consideration for the next closer (BC) seat.
- Merch.
- **"Do two jobs at once":** keep SDR KPIs while closing for yourself (every entrepreneur does today's job and tomorrow's job).
- Story: a future sales director was told to **self-source and close** a gym owner. His managers kept moving the bar ("that one was already in your pipeline", "that was luck") until he punched a wall. His dad pointed out they were testing how badly he wanted it, so he closed two more and got the seat. **Force leadership's hand.**
- Then: memorize the closer handbook → the **7-day closer bootcamp** (same format) over a ~30-day transition, while keeping SDR duties.
- **Closer ramp gates:**
- 2–3 self-set closes/week for 3 straight weeks.
- Low-quality outbound leads set by SDRs. Need >60% show, ~90% on-rate and **>30% close** to move to medium/high-quality outbound.
- **Inbound rotation** (ads/organic), allocated by the manager to the top performer on the outbound calendar.
- **Stimulant rule:** the amount of caffeine and nicotine should go down as ticket size and nuance go up. New closers detox for 7–14 days so they slow down and sell from the back foot, without pressure or "commission breath".

## ---

**Culture**

- At Gym Launch, Alex cut a team from **14 people to 5 and sales went up**. The A-players stepped up, and the remaining reps got more deals. **Culture is the most fragile thing in a sales department. No single rep is worth more than the culture.** The hardest cuts are bad people who are making you money; they cost the most because they keep everyone else from growing.
- **"The worst person on your team is your real standard."** If you can't tell what's wrong with a team, look at the leader. Most sales leaders are mediocre, and a world-class team needs a world-class leader.
- Reinforce what you want and ignore or punish what you don't. Hire people with similar goals and tie each behaviour to their personal goal and to the company vision.
- **Operationalize the "psycho".** Alex's first one bought leads with his own money to be #1. Now **every closer does 2 hours of outbound a day** at the best pickup hours (for ACQ, 2–4pm PT, blocked on the calendar). Those deals pay **double commission** and cost ACQ no marketing. This keeps closers sharp and shows setters that closers grind too. A drop in self-sets is a leading indicator of laziness. **Self-sets alone should cover a closer's salary.**
- **Written standard: a closer handbook (~26k words)** holding the career path, schedule, every skill and script, and the team's lore. Every time a good rep churns, add the lesson to it. Lore stories:
- **"Garbage man"**: a new closer took everyone's junk leads as free practice. "Sharpen the sword": take every call.
- **"Yellows are gold"**: a rookie worked the unloved mid-score yellow leads and out-closed everyone. **Volume negates luck.**
- Reps dial 200–400 times a day. They're professionals, and professionals practise (Kobe, MJ).
- **Leaderboards are mandatory**: visible, accurate, real-time, with real outcomes (bonuses, shout-outs, a **belt** for #1).
- v1: a Slack bot posting each close.
- v2: a TV on the wall.
- Low-tech: poster, bell.
- **Daily 5 non-negotiables (all reps)**, each screenshotted into the team thread for kudos:
- 20 minutes consuming Alex's content (prospect/product fluency).
- 1 role-play.
- 1 game tape or shadow.
- A workout.
- Closers: outbound block. SDRs: 50 pipeline dials.
- Dialers max out at **2 lines** so ACQ doesn't burn high-value leads. Cheap leads can justify more.

## The manager's day (revenue-generating activities)

- **~6:00 Review results and today's calls**:
- Look at each funnel separately and scrub fake or test bookings so the data is true.
- Check lead quality.
- Set stretch targets and update the leaderboard.
- Check calendar capacity.
- Make sure reps nurtured today's calls and wrote call notes.
- **Send daily feedback to marketing on lead quality.**
- **Onboarding hour** (cohort bootcamp, days 1–14).
- **Kickoff prep**: pull call attributions, a customer testimonial and **one specific behaviour shout-out**.
- **Kickoff (daily huddle): the most important meeting.** Run it at the slowest call time.
- **Daily theme mapped to the script**:
- Mon: Intro
- Tue: Disco
- Wed: Pitch
- Thu: Close
- Fri: **Hot topic** (the week's biggest sticking point or a seasonal issue). If there isn't one, run **"popcorn" role-play**: the manager plays the prospect and calls on reps at random.
- Sat: **Pipeline review** (5–10 minutes moving deals forward).
- **Agenda**: peer shout-outs → customer testimonial (reminds reps the work changes lives) → script training → role-play.
- Shout-outs must be **behaviour-specific**. Not "Josh had a great day", but "Josh created urgency with a prospect who tried to brush him off, and used the 'can I be frank — this is a priorities issue, not timing' challenge." Keep it under 5 minutes.
- Role-play: point out the single biggest issue, model it, practise it, and explain why it matters for the rep's goals.
- **Sales is a perishable skill.** Skipping training is never allowed, except when a closing call runs over.
- **Office hours** for extra training. Setter and closer managers attend each other's huddles.
- **Sales interviews** every day, to keep talent pressure on.
- **"Looking for dead bodies"** (pipeline inspection): stalled opportunities, forgotten leads, missed callbacks, **unworked referrals**, no-shows, messy handoffs. Assign an owner and a next step to each.
- **Live listens ("eye of Sauron")**: the manager can whisper into any live call, so reps always feel watched (the secret-shopper effect), and shouts out good handling in real time ("catch them doing it right").
- CRM and tech hygiene (clean the CRM, audit workflows, remove spam-flagged numbers, **audit speed-to-lead by tier**).
- Group call reviews and role-plays, a second onboarding block, ad-hoc 1:1 game tape for underperformers.
- **End of day**: admin checks (tracking sheets, outcomes, notes for tomorrow, nurture texts sent). The report goes to leadership and marketing via a form feeding a dashboard.

## SDR targets & weekly 1:1

- **SDR targets**:
- ~50 sets/month.
- Show rate >70% (60% is the ungate floor).
- 10+ closes/month generated, at roughly **5 sets per close** (great reps hit 2.5–3:1).
- 13+ deals/month unlocks the top commission (~$10–12k/month,~$120–148k/year).
- **Weekly 1:1**:
- **The rep fills in the template 30+ minutes ahead.** Not preparing is a cultural red flag.
- The manager reviews data and **hunts their own calls** (reps only send their good ones).
- **Structure**:
  1. Personal check-in, handled first if something's wrong.
  2. Last week's focus: did the number move, and why?
  3. Data vs team average across the funnel.
  4. **One focus: one KPI + the behaviour that drives it** (never 10 things).
  5. Define "done" and the measurable outcome.
  6. Written commitments with dates, plus game tape or office hours.
- If someone has been crushing it for ~3 months, switch to **long-term career aspirations** (e.g. sit in on marketing or on Alex's client meetings).
- **Manager cheat sheet: metric → root cause → fix**:
- **Dials low** (activity): bad scheduling or inefficient dialling → fixed dial blocks, time coaching. **No victory laps**: the best time to close is right after a close.
- **Connect rate low**: usually systems (spam flags, recycled numbers, slow speed-to-lead, bad time of day, over-worked lists) → dial sprints at peak hours, check the dialer and the list. **Skipped dials faked as dials = instant firing.**
- **Connect → conversation (>3 minutes) low**: weak first 30 seconds (flat or robotic tone, no clear ask, early objections) → game-tape the first 30 seconds of many calls, role-play "30 seconds to see if this is even relevant?" and the brush-offs.
- **Conversation → set low**: weak disco (no clear desired state, or no obstacle) → find on tape where the rep stopped digging; role-play drawing out the desired state, then "what's in the way?"
- **Show rate low**: poor qualification, too long between booking and call, bad time slot, VSL not watched → check BANT, **book same or next day (max 4 days out)**, book a time when the owner can focus, faster speed-to-lead, and the closer jumps into a 3-way chat right away.
- **BANT**:
- **Budget**: don't set people who can't invest.
- **Authority**: a solo owner is ideal; otherwise get all decision makers on the call, or have them watch the VSL and frame the next call as a fit call.
- **Need**: a desired state in their own words plus a real obstacle.
- **Timing**: they want it solved ASAP.
- Ask for **deal-breakers** (logistics vs value) before finalizing. ACQ also shares a free AI skill that grades calls for BANT.

## Closers: Hunt mode vs Kill mode

- **Max opportunities × max conversion = max sales.** Hunt is everything off the call; Kill is everything on it. Every hour should be designated as one or the other.
- **HUNT**:
- **Call notes**: an AI skill turns any call transcript into a ~6-line CRM note, so the next person has full context in 30 seconds. Prospects hate re-explaining, and you go in with intel (personality type, likely objections, so you can bring matching proof). Setters fill them in; closers complete them the night before and the morning of.
- **Work the list in priority order**:
- **P1 inbound sets**:
- Double-dial immediately and **try to pull the call forward**: "Would it be crazy if we did it right now?" This lifts show rate (now = 100%, same-day > later), close rate (in the moment) and utilization; keeps momentum; and saves all the reminder work.
- If there's no pickup, text in 3 blocks: what's going on with [problem], check the pre-call material, I have X or Y today.
- "Looking forward to our call tomorrow" wording gets past smartphone spam filters.
- No reply after 12h: "prepping, could you check my last message?" 24h before: "finished prepping, someone's asking for that slot, thumbs up to hold it." 12h before: cancel ("life gets busy") and rebook. Better to reschedule than eat a dead hour.
- **"A no-show is not a no."** Don't get self-righteous: "Looks like we got our wires crossed." Offer two times. Week 1: 1 call + 1 text a day. Week 2: lighter. Then the value ladder.
- **P1 outbound sets**:
- The setter hands off immediately with the VSL ("saves time on your call"). **The closer replies within minutes** and owns the chat; the setter rebooks any no-shows.
- Morning of: send a testimonial from someone with the same problem, **highlighting the relevant part**. One hour before: "talk soon".
- **P2 BAMFAMs**: proof matched to their objection, a value message 3 days out, reminders the night before and morning of.
- **P3 pipeline** (showed but didn't close, newest → oldest, 60 days back). **Value ladder**, one rung at a time:
- Value ("you mentioned X, a customer just sent me this").
- "What questions came up?"
- Bump ("John?").
- "Should I assume this isn't a priority right now?"
- Re-offer ("an opening came up this week — grab it before I give it away?").
- Always double-dial before texting. Colour-code lead status. "No prospect left behind." There's usually about a deal a day hiding in the list.
- **Outbound block (2h minimum)**:
- **Priority 1: referrals** (30%+ of sales, the highest return on time). Ask buyers you didn't have time to ask, and anyone who sends a nice text.
- **Compliment** ("if we could talk only to people like you all day, we would") → "**who else do you know who's as successful as you?**" → "**You're not against putting us in a group text?**" (a negatively framed question) → **give them the exact words to paste** → "anyone else?" (the best time for a referral is right after one) → if no: "Alex would kill me if I didn't ask… how about someone less successful than you?"
- Never be afraid to ask; it makes you look more dialled in.
- **Priority 2: unscheduled opt-ins**, newest first. Expect ~2 sets/hour, so ~4 sets → ~1 close. Referrals plus opt-ins should give ~**2 deals/day per closer from outbound**. Any free time goes to self-setting.
- **End-of-day checklist (~60 minutes, or zero if done right after each call)**:
- Mark CRM outcomes (closed / BAMFAM / pipeline / opt-out) so the dialer auto-prioritizes.
- Update call notes.
- Handle compliance opt-outs.
- **Submit your worst call of the day** for review (5 a week).
- **Inbox zero** across channels.
- Closer schedule: the only hard blocks are call notes, outbound and training. **Daily max 20 scheduled calls (≈12–15 live).** Gaps in the calendar get filled with the priority list.
- **KILL mode diagnostics.** If qualified people show up and don't buy, it's one of three things:
- **The offer sucks**: fix the offer, not the rep.
- **They're not ready**: long calls and lots of questions. Fix with a VSL at every step, a multi-call agenda set up front, and specific proof between calls.
- **The rep sucks at sales**: trace it through Intro / Disco / Pitch / Close.
- **Intro failures**:
- The prospect opens with "so what's this about?" — the rep didn't set or own the agenda, or set it apologetically.
- The rep never got agreement on the agenda. "Sound good?" is the first, lowest-stakes yes.
- The prospect re-explains what they told the setter — read the notes; remembered details build influence.
- **Disco: get a "hell yes" on a crystal-clear problem** before moving on. Lawyers don't ask questions they don't know the answer to.
- Vague goals don't motivate. Get numbers and emotions.
- Don't accept surface goals ("more leads"). Go 1–2 levels deeper: "what would that do for you? give me an example."
- Rushing to the offer means fear of hard questions.
- Rep talking too much: in disco you only ask questions.
- Make them attach **money, a quantity, a timeline or a person** ("I lost $40k in 6 months and had to lay off my brother").
- If they say "that's exactly my problem", they'll almost certainly buy (if qualified).
- **Pitch failures**:
- Running past 2 minutes (features, jargon, being "cute"). Use one analogy or story and follow the script.
- Mentioning things they never asked about creates objections. Map only what solves their stated problem; keep the rest in your back pocket.
- Trailing off, or talking after the ask. **Ask and zip it: whoever speaks first after the ask gets sold.**
- **Close/loop failures**:
- Answering the literal objection ("I need to think about it") instead of isolating it: confirm value → "what's the main variable / what are you afraid of?"
- Stopping after one objection. Stack and loop, peeling the onion; fake objections come before the real one.
- Asking only twice, or getting argumentative to be right. **An objection is a buying signal** (uninterested people just leave). "Totally, and…" (AAA). Keep your tone constant and stay in the pocket.
- **Tonality**: "I didn't say he hit his dog" means something different depending on which word you stress. Every word in the script has a job.
- Speak at **150–170 words per minute**, loud, and enunciate (pronouncing vowels naturally slows you down).
- Raise your pitch on questions (marked "?" in the script). Use the scripted short, medium and long pauses.
- **Pausing 8+ seconds after the ask = ~23–40% more closes.** You'll lose up to 40% of deals if you don't shut up.
- **Closer 1:1**: the manager reviews ~3 calls with a **scorecard for each script element** and drills the weakest ("if you do this, then this happens"). Saturday: a 15-minute red/yellow/green pipeline review with the last message and next step.

## Monthly all-team meeting (30 minutes, in person + Zoom)

- Agenda → team-to-team kudos → each team's wins and improvements → **kudos for the top 3 and a belt ceremony for #1** → opportunities for next month → resell the vision (new products, lead magnets, company growth = their opportunity).
- **Belt and promotions are the biggest reinforcement events. Tie each one explicitly to the behaviours that earned it** ("Dylan was an SDR, did X, became a closer, did Y, got the belt").

## Closing thoughts

- Ignore the mediocre. Unlock what you want by trying **10–100× harder**, not 1.5×. Become obsessed and min-max rather than balance.
- **Sales is the universal skill**: you're always selling investors, your team, prospects, change, a vision. It still matters in an AI world.
- Mastery takes ~**10,000 conversations**. The only question is how fast. **Tie career milestones to lifetime volume** (100 / 300 / 500 deals closed), not tenure.
- Build a culture you're proud of; the mechanics follow.

## Sales & Closing

271 ideas from 107 videos. [#N] = video N in the Start here tab.

- Build a choreographed sales process by trial and error, then reverse-engineer the steps that led to a purchase and script them so non-founder reps can repeat it. [▶ 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VBoRLJimVzc)
- Selling is the escape skill: start by selling someone else's product, then learn to buy cheap and flip, and trade up to bigger items over time (cards to furniture to homes), eventually selling your own thing. [▶ 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YFA8AS5Cu2w)
- AI sales agents trained on millions of calls could run conversations 24/7 with more "experience" than any human rep; a Google demo already booked a haircut by phone years ago. [▶ 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KYqEK_T_5M4)
- Proof beats promise: the same product with 1,000 testimonials outsells a fancy offer with none. Better proof is recent, visual (video weigh-ins beat text), high-volume (screenshot every review and cover a lobby wall), and starts with the customer's pain. Ask for testimonials at peak satisfaction; sell at peak deprivation. [▶ 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oRMG_HpOAN4)
- CLOSER framework: Clarify why they came, Label the problem, Overview past attempts (the pain cycle that raises deprivation), Sell the vacation (outcomes, usually a three-point pitch, not features), Explain away concerns (time, money, decision maker, avoidance, specifics), Reinforce the decision with a strong first 24 hours. [▶ 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oRMG_HpOAN4)
- Nearly every self-made millionaire he knows started in high-volume sales (door knocking, cold calling, in-person) for three to five years; sales skills transfer to negotiating, dating and leadership. His early appointment-setting tips: open with the person's name as a question, keep a playful high-energy tone, and he even bounced on a small trampoline between calls to stay energized. [▶ 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aFoMYz_jWcs)
- Avoid the feast-and-famine cycle: when content and outreach bring sales, people ease off, cash dries up, and they restart in scarcity. Keep the activities constant whether results are good or not yet good. [▶ 11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7ITff1fIbSc)
- Target the right buyer for the premium tier (a different person from your $100 customer) and describe their pain more precisely than they can; mining reviews of popular books in your niche (now easier with AI) gives you their exact language. Specific pain often persuades better than a bigger promise. [▶ 13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI)
- People act only to gain good things or avoid bad ones, so also describe the downside you remove: risks avoided, slowness avoided, things they would normally have to start doing (waking early to work out) and things they would have to give up (taco Tuesdays). Specific pain (e.g. chafing thighs in the sun) beats vague promises like "lose weight fast." [▶ 14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nIk3DedjxJM)
- Frustration tolerance, the number of rejections you can take and still try again, is a learnable skill; in business, nobody counts how many doors you knock on, and volume eventually opens one. [▶ 15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UDBkiBnMrHs)
- Negotiate everything except your values; most offers are a first guess, so ask what problem each side is solving. Avoid squeezing vendors for every penny; balance your needs and theirs both today and in 10 years for loyal relationships. [▶ 16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cq8GyLrEuAk)
- Proof over promise: a seller with thousands of reviews at 4.7 beats a bigger promise with one review. Before launching anything, work free for beta users in exchange for testimonials, reviews and feedback; do epic things first, then talk about them. [▶ 17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HxEQCHpZzHk)
- The first skill to learn is selling, because with zero sales nothing else matters. Every skill you add raises your income floor (e.g., marketing plus sales means you could always make around $1M/yr by getting leads for local businesses and closing them). [▶ 22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Nh8Oc7ERdIU)
- Have no shame about outreach when you need money: knock, call, email, DM, ask. Every attempt pays off asymmetrically, with either a sale or a lesson. Shame means breaking other people's rules, so ask whose rules you're following. Usually it's one or two specific people's opinions holding you back. [▶ 24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MzAIP_WJ-jE)
- To collect more cash sooner, raise prices or sell more right away: prepay quarterly at a small discount (built into the price), and add onboarding or bundles up front. Ignore "industry standard" net-60 billing. The pay-before-work spectrum runs from wage earner to contractor to surgeon to insurer to royalty holder. [▶ 25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k-3PoOT4vOM)
- Result: summer camp revenue was up 325% year over year, but the tiny sales team couldn't call all the leads. As long as you have lead flow, salespeople pay for themselves, so hiring them is low-risk growth spending. The plan from there was to repeat the giveaway play year-round for birthdays at a smaller budget. [▶ 26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xRxVpjeHmeA)
- Step 5, when someone replies, warm them up with ACA: Acknowledge something about them, Compliment it, then Ask a question tied to that compliment that leads naturally toward the problem you solve (e.g., a busy working mom: how does she find time to eat well and exercise?). [▶ 28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w7g08dVTwaE)
- Referral script: a referral ask: whether they know someone with problem X who wants result Y, mentioning a few free case-study spots and a recent similar win If they say no, ask jokingly whether anyone they dislike comes to mind. The short version: I help [avatar] get [dream outcome] in [time] without [effort], guaranteed [risk reversal]. [▶ 28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w7g08dVTwaE)
- Give value with no strings attached instead of offering it "in exchange for" something. Do excellent work for about 100 people ahead of you; a few will offer paid work or a job, which is how much of his team was hired. His first clients came through a charity model: they donated to charity in exchange for 12 weeks of training, and many then paid him to continue. [▶ 31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ln24y0FPJHo)
- Selling is helping prospects make a decision for themselves, not getting a purchase. Power means shrinking the gap between thought and action. Emotion lowers the threshold to act, but logic is what keeps the buyer from regretting it, so answer both. [▶ 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NcD2t9qt-fM)
- Core beliefs: prospects want to believe you; selling happens before the ask and closing happens after it; expect "no", because if they could decide alone they wouldn't need you; if nobody gasps at your price, it's too low, and a high anchor makes later prices feel small. Stay curious rather than argumentative ("huh, tell me more"). Record every sale so you can study your hot streaks and train new reps. [▶ 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NcD2t9qt-fM)
- Selling is transferring belief across a bridge of trust. Cold streaks usually come from lost conviction, not lost skill, so refill your belief. People can sense whether you want to help them or just close them. Whoever cares most about the prospect, sometimes more than the prospect does, wins. [▶ 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NcD2t9qt-fM)
- Closing is the "red zone." He cites the stat that the top five NFL red-zone offenses made the playoffs 90% of the time, and strong closing covers many other weaknesses. Of 100 prospects, about 10% always buy, 10% never will, and the fight is over the middle 80%. [▶ 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NcD2t9qt-fM)
- Obstacles come up before the ask (e.g., "just wanted info"), and you should clear them early. Objections come after the ask. Before closing, confirm three beliefs: the product gets them the goal in the way they want (gym prospects who refused training still bought supplements); others will support them; and it will work for them specifically. Pile on proof until not believing becomes unreasonable. [▶ 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NcD2t9qt-fM)
- Objections are reality distortions (borrowing from CBT's three core irrational beliefs) that blame circumstances, other people, or the self. Peel them like an onion from the outside in: time, then money, then fit, then authority, then avoidance ("I need to think about it"), which is the core. [▶ 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NcD2t9qt-fM)
- Time: you'll always be busy, so learn the habit now while you have support. Micro version: "I complained too, until my wife showed me my phone's screen time," and a good program removes work rather than adding it. The "when-then" fallacy: "I'll buy the thing that makes money once I have money." [▶ 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NcD2t9qt-fM)
- Money: if it feels like a lot, that's good, because they'll commit harder. It's small relative to the result (e.g., +$10K/month) and versus alternatives like a four-year degree. You'll pay either way, in money now or in years of trial and error; buying other people's lessons is how you buy time. Resourcefulness beats resources (Nike's founder got vendors to cover payroll), and everyone finds money for an unexpected tax bill. [▶ 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NcD2t9qt-fM)
- Fit: a new identity brings new priorities (like teens told to start budgeting for makeup). You have to change the habits that produced the current result. Ask whether staying the same hurts more than changing. Hypotheticals: a question asking whether they would buy if it were perfect, and what would make it so Then swap the detail they disliked. [▶ 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NcD2t9qt-fM)
- Authority/spouse: isolate the objection by asking what the partner wouldn't like, then handle that. Do they approve of the current struggle? Would you support them in the same situation? Ask the partner for support, not permission, to avoid later resentment. A short no-questions guarantee helps. [▶ 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NcD2t9qt-fM)
- Avoidance: it isn't a fast decision, since they've been making it for years. Name the sunk cost of getting this far. Ask "What are you most afraid of if you buy?" "Don't let a bad past purchase burn you twice." The rocking-chair close: life will make the decision for them, and decisions need information, not time, with you as the source. Confirm three yeses (it works, you trust me, it'll work for you) plus access to the money, then lay out the options. With a guarantee, the only guaranteed failure is walking away. [▶ 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NcD2t9qt-fM)
- CLOSER framework: Clarify why they're here; Label the problem (current state, desired state, the obstacle in between); Overview past pain (what they tried, why it failed) to widen the gap; Sell the vacation, a three-pillar pitch with an analogy per pillar, focused on the destination rather than the process; Explain away concerns (time, money, authority, fit, past bad experiences, stalling); Reinforce the decision. [▶ 34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AN2KpRBsmRY)
- A salesperson's three jobs: maximize opportunities, convert the highest percentage, and keep doing it for a long time. Across about 4,000 appointments/day in his software data, the strongest predictor of total sales was the number of available time slots. Be open when prospects are free, including weekends and same-day. [▶ 35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JE2_7elAcxM)
- Calendar tactics: pull later appointments into today's open slots (same-day shows and closes better). Call a new booking right away and either close then or move them into an earlier slot; one solar rep sold about 4x the next best this way. Cancel and refill unconfirmed slots. Have an off-call SOP as well as the on-call script. Book a meeting from every meeting. Keep a "kill list" of whale prospects. [▶ 35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JE2_7elAcxM)
- Referrals: ask "Who do you know who's as awesome as you and would benefit?" (the question demands a name, not a yes/no). One new rep beat the team by 50% just by asking every buyer who else wants to come; referrals close at around 80-90%. Before calls, ask a preference question (shirt size, choice of gift card) to raise show rates. [▶ 35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JE2_7elAcxM)
- Prep roughly 10% of the meeting length for routine calls (6 minutes for an hour) and more for rare, high-stakes ones. Five minutes of research on the prospect builds instant rapport. Take notes so the next call never asks the prospect to repeat themselves, and so recommendations feel contextual (which reads as consultant, not salesperson). [▶ 35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JE2_7elAcxM)
- The best reps listen about twice as much as they talk (per call-AI data). Answer questions with questions, since prospects believe what they say, not what you say. Use commands like "Tell me about your day" to break autopilot. Know the script so well you "breathe" it. Keep wording concise; scripts bloat when reps add superstitious steps after lucky closes. Drill one line at a time in daily role-plays. [▶ 35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JE2_7elAcxM)
- Handle obstacles before you state the price ("kill zombies up front"). Play the objection out into the past and future with a story (a prospect who waited on her husband and was still stuck years later).
